parole.testo: From German Abort, itself derived from Latin abortiō. In the computing sense: from English abort.
Borrowed from German Akazie, from Latin acacia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía).
Borrowed from German Aquamarin, from Latin aqua marīna (“sea water”).
Borrowed from German Antiquar, from Latin antiquarius.
From German Anthrazit, from Latin anthracītis, from Ancient Greek ἀνθρακῖτις (anthrakîtis).
Borrowed from German Artefakt. Further from Latin ars + Latin factus.
Borrowed from German Artikel, from Latin articulus; attested 1704. Displaced the earlier form арты́кул (artýkul), which was borrowed from Polish artykuł. Doublet of арти́кль (artíklʹ).
Borrowed from German Archiv, from Latin archīvum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon).
Borrowed from German Asyndeton, from Latin asyndeton, from Ancient Greek ἀσύνδετον (asúndeton). Compare with бессою́зие (bessojúzije).
Borrowed from German Balsam, from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon, “balsam”).
Borrowed from German Virus, from Latin vīrus.
Borrowed from German General, further from Latin generālis.

parole.significato: a genius (someone possessing extraordinary mental capacity)
parole.testo: First attested 1763. Borrowed from German Genius or directly from Latin genius. Displaced the earlier form гениуш, which was borrowed from Polish. Compare typologically саморо́док (samoródok), прирождённый (priroždjónnyj).
Borrowed from German Honorar, eventually from Latin honōrārium.
Borrowed from German Granat, from Latin pomum granatum (“grainy apple”).

parole.significato: dean (senior official in college or university)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Dekan, from Late Latin decānus.
Borrowed from German Dekanat, from Dechanat, from Medieval Latin decanatus, from decanus.

Borrowed from German Divis (whence also Polish dywiz), from Latin dīvīsus, from Latin dīvidō. Doublet of деви́з (devíz), дивиде́нд (dividénd), and диви́зия (divízija). Compare Slovene deljaj (“hyphen”) (akin to Russian дели́ть (delítʹ)). On the other hand compare Czech spojovník (“hyphen”), Serbo-Cr

Borrowed from German Dialektik, from Late Latin dialectica, from Ancient Greek διαλεκτική (dialektikḗ, “the art of argument through interactive questioning and answering”), from διαλεκτικός (dialektikós, “relating to dialogue”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to participate in a dialogue”), from διά
Perhaps borrowed from German Dysenterie; ultimately from Latin dysenteria, from Ancient Greek δυσεντερία (dusentería).

Borrowed from German Dilettant. Ultimately from Latin dēlectō (whence also English delight). Further from Latin dē- + Latin laciō (the ultimate source of Russian делика́тный (delikátnyj), Russian деликате́с (delikatés)).
Borrowed from German Direktor. From Late Latin dīrēctor, from Latin dīrēctus, from Latin dīrigō.
Borrowed from German Salve, from Latin salve.

Borrowed from German isolieren, German isolieren + -овать (-ovatʹ) (per Shansky, however, French isoler + -овать (-ovatʹ)). Omitting several steps, from Latin īnsula (whence also и́нсула (ínsula), инсули́н (insulín)).
Borrowed in the 18th century from German Inventar (“inventory”), from Latin inventārium; suffix influenced by -а́рь (-árʹ).
Borrowed from German Kolophonium, from Latin colophonium, from Ancient Greek κολοφωνία (kolophōnía), from Κολοφων (Kolophōn, “town in Lydia”).

parole.significato: chancellor (title of various high-ranking politicians or academic officials, including heads of government in Germany a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Kanzler, from Late Latin cancellarius.

parole.significato: scorifier, capsule (small porous thick-walled cup made of pressed bone ash, used for purifying gold from oxidizable met…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Kapelle, probably from New Latin cupella, diminutive of Latin cupa (“cup”).
Borrowed from German kapitulieren (“to capitulate”), from Latin capitulare, from capitulum, diminutive form of caput, from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *káput (“head”).
Borrowed from German Kappe, ultimately from Late Latin cappa. Doublet of ка́па (kápa) and ша́пка (šápka).
Borrowed from German kaputt. Further from Latin cappa. Doublet of капо́т (kapót), капюшо́н (kapjušón), ке́пка (képka), and ша́пка (šápka).
From German Kommissar, from Latin commissus.
From German Kondensator, from Latin condēnsō (“to thicken”).
Per Vasmer, from German Konditer, popular variant of Konditor, from Latin condītor.
Probable, borrowing from German Kontrapunkt, from Medieval Latin contrapunctum.
First borrowed from German Konfekt in the form of конфе́кта (konfékta) in the 16th century, ultimately from Latin cōnfectus. Later influenced by or borrowed again from Italian confetto.
Borrowed from German Krematorium, from New Latin crematorium.
Borrowed in the early 18th century from German Kubus or directly from Latin cubus, from Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos, “die, cube”).
Borrowed from German Lawine. Further from Latin lābīna, from lābor. Compare typologically о́ползень (ópolzenʹ) (< ползти́ (polztí)).
Borrowed from German Lätzchen. Ultimately from Latin laqueus. Doublet of лассо́ (lassó).
Borrowed from German Lyzeum, from Latin lyceum.

Borrowed from German Lunatiker (“sleepwalker”), from Latin lūnāticus, from lūna. Compare Macedonian месечар (mesečar), Serbo-Croatian ме̏сеча̄р, related to Macedonian месечина (mesečina), Serbo-Croatian ме̏се̄ц, Russian ме́сяц (mésjac).

parole.significato: Moor (a member of a certain mixed race of Arab and Berber people)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Maure or Latin Maurus. Doublet of му́рин (múrin).

parole.significato: wastepaper (unwanted paper that has been discarded)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Makulatur, from Latin maculātūra. Further from Latin maculō, from Latin macula, related to Ancient Greek σμάω (smáō) (whence σμῆγμα (smêgma) and σμηκτικός (smēktikós)).

parole.significato: mystery (secret rite in Ancient Greece and Rome)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Mysterium, from Latin mysterium, from Ancient Greek μυστήριον (mustḗrion).
Borrowed from German Monarch, itself derived from Latin monarcha, in turn derived from Ancient Greek μόναρχος (mónarkhos). Attested since the 16th century.

Borrowed from German Oval or French ovale, from Medieval Latin ovālis, from Latin ōvum. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm (whence also Ancient Greek ᾠόν (ōión), English egg, Russian яйцо (jajco)).
Perhaps German operativ + -ный (-nyj). Further from Latin operātīvus, from Latin operō (< Latin opus, akin to ops).
Borrowed from German Orden. Further from Latin ōrdō.
Borrowed from German Offerte, ultimately from Late Latin offerta, from Vulgar Latin *offerīre.
Borrowed from German Parität, itself from Late Latin paritas.

parole.significato: cartridge, shell, or round, consisting of the assembled bullet, casing, propellant, and primer
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Patrone. Omitting several steps, from Latin patrōnus, from Latin pater.

parole.significato: pencil case, pencil box (object purposed to contain stationery)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Pennal. Further derived from Latin penna (whence English pen), from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én-, from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂-.
Borrowed from German Pietät, from Latin pietās (whence also English piety, English pity).

parole.significato: a prepared specimen; a specimen mounted on a microscope slide
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Präparat, from Latin praeparātiō. Compare to English preparation.
From German provozieren, itself derived from Latin provocare.
Borrowed from German Prospekt, from Latin prōspectus (“view, sight”).
From профо́с (profós), from German Profoss. Ultimately from Latin praepositus (whence also English provost).
Borrowed from German Prozent, ultimately from New Latin per centum. First attested 1724.
Borrowed from German Pult, from Latin pulpitum (“platform, scaffold”).
Borrowed from German Puppe. Further from Latin pūpus (via pūpa).
Borrowed from German Purpur, from Latin purpura, from Ancient Greek πορφύρα (porphúra); cognate with English purple.
Borrowed from German Rarität, from Latin raritas ≃ rarus (“rare”).
Borrowed from German Regent, further from Latin regēns.
Borrowed from German reduzieren, further from Latin redūcere.
Borrowed from German Rekognoszierung (“reconnaissance”), from Latin recognosco.
Borrowed from German Rezept, from Latin receptus.
Borrowed from German Rezeptur, from Latin receptūra.
Borrowed from German Rezeption, from Latin receptiō. Doublet of ресе́пшен (resépšen).
Borrowed from German simulieren, from Latin simulō and German -ieren, with the Russian suffix -овать (-ovatʹ). Morphologically симул- + -и́ровать (-írovatʹ).
Borrowed from German Sinekure, from Latin sine (“without”) + cūra (“care”).
Borrowed from German Strauß. Further from Latin strūthiō.
Borrowed from German Szene, from Latin scaena. Further from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).
Borrowed from German Taxe, from Medieval Latin taxa.
Borrowed from German Termin, from Medieval Latin terminus.
Borrowed from German Technik, from Latin technica, from Ancient Greek τεχνική (tekhnikḗ).
Borrowed from German Tyrann, from Latin tyrannus, from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos).
Borrowed from German Traktat, from Latin tractātus.
Borrowed from German transzendental; ultimately from Latin trānscendēns (“transcending”).
Borrowed from German Tumbe (“grave, coffin”), from Vulgar Latin tumba (“grave”). Compare typologically бюст (bjust) << Latin bustum.
Borrowed from German Universität, from Latin ūniversitās.
Borrowed from German Fabrikant, ultimately from Latin fabrica. Cognate with фа́брика (fábrika).
Borrowed from German Phase, from Latin phasis, from Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis). Doublet of фа́зис (fázis).
Borrowed from German Fasan, from Latin phasianus, from Ancient Greek φασιανός (phasianós, “bird of the river Φᾶσις (Phâsis)”).

parole.significato: torch (a stick with a flame at one end)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Fackel, from Middle High German vackel, from Old High German faccala, from Latin facula.
Borrowed from German Fenchel, ultimately from Latin fēnuculum.

Borrowed from German violett. Further from Latin viola (whence also фиа́лка (fiálka)). Compare typologically ро́зовый (rózovyj) (< ро́за (róza)), лило́вый (lilóvyj) (akin to ли́лия (lílija)). Also note цвет (cvet), цвето́к (cvetók).

parole.significato: fortochka (a small ventilation window spanning the frame of one window pane, opening independently of the whole window)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Pförtchen (“little door”), diminutive of Pforte (“gate”), an ancient borrowing from Latin porta (“gate”).

parole.significato: front (large operational military command that controls several armies; equivalent to U.S. army group)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Front. Omitting several steps, from Latin frōns, frontis.
Borrowed from German Chronik, from Latin chronica, from Ancient Greek χρονικός (khronikós), from χρόνος (khrónos), of unknown origin.
Borrowed from German Zentner. Further from Latin centēnārius, from centēnus, from Latin centum.
Borrowed from German Zylinder, from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros).
Borrowed from German Zyniker, from Latin cynicus.
Borrowed from German Zirkel, from Latin circulus.
Borrowed from German Zirkular (“circular (notice for mass distribution)”), from Latin circulāris.

parole.significato: quote, quotation, citation (a statement attributed to someone)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Zitat, ultimately from Latin citō (whence ultimately also English citation).
From German zitieren + -овать (-ovatʹ), from Latin citāre, from ciēre, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey-.

parole.significato: scale (a graph or instrument depicting a sequence of numbers used to measure quantity or quality)
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Skala. Further from Latin scāla, from Latin scandō.
Borrowed from German Äquator, from Medieval Latin aequātor. Compare Ukrainian еква́тор (ekvátor), Belarusian эква́тар (ekvátar).
Borrowed from German Äquivalent, itself from Latin aequivalentem, accusative singular of aequivalēns, present active participle of aequivaleō (“to be equivalent, have equal power”).
Borrowed from German experimentieren, from Latin experimentare. For the suffix, see -и́ровать (-írovatʹ).
First attested in 1704. Borrowed from German Jurist, from Medieval Latin iūrista.
